topic: robotics; embodied AI; social navigation; robot safety
status: candidate research opportunity from four fixed-frame audits; proposes cross-task evaluation, not a claim that existing safety metrics are absent
claim: In this sampled slice, robot systems use distinct outcome families: task success in simulated sparse-reward benchmarks, social disturbance in human-centered navigation, object tracking/search time, and physical contact/impact in acrobatics. These outcomes are not interchangeable. The VAPS study makes the tradeoff explicit: under one simulation threshold, head and hand contact drop sharply while maneuver success also declines slightly; GSON measures social disturbance alongside motion quality; HiER's strong success-rate evidence is simulation-only. A useful opportunity is to evaluate task progress and task-specific harm together in matched physical scenarios, rather than rank systems using success alone. This does not imply that the four papers or the wider field lack such measures.
positive_evidence: VAPS full-hierarchy simulation on Unitree G1 reports head contact falling 27.7% to 1.6% and hand contact 36.6% to 8.8%, while success moves from 62.1% to 59.6%; physical full-hierarchy evaluation is 15/18 successful specialist objectives on LimX Oli.

GSON explicitly measures individual/group disturbance and comfort distance in addition to conventional motion metrics; it reports lower selected social-disturbance measures, but each physical scenario has only three runs and dense-crowd latency/occlusion failures remain.

LOVON reports a 6-m Go2 backpack-search improvement from 178s to 32.57s with its extra state plus blur filter, making perception loss/search time visible rather than collapsing everything into success.
HiER reports an aggregate IQM success-rate increase from 0.56 to 0.83 for a matched SAC+HER comparison over eight simulated tasks, but does not test physical transfer.
counterevidence: GSON already demonstrates a multi-objective design by measuring social disturbance and standard navigation metrics together; VAPS reports an explicit Pareto frontier between task success and head-contact rate.
VAPS includes some physical hardware evidence and GSON/LOVON include real robot trials, so it would be inaccurate to call all embodied evidence simulation-only.
The four systems solve different tasks and should not be forced into a universal scalar harm measure; harm definitions need to remain task- and stakeholder-specific.

sources.sections: Go2 ablation, simulator outcomes, real-world evaluation
Unitree G1 safety/success results and LimX Oli trials

falsifiable_test: Preregister a physical-robot benchmark spanning at least three task families (navigation around people, long-horizon object search, and dynamic manipulation/acrobatics) and multiple conditions per task. For every run report task success/progress, completion time, task-specific harms (social disturbance, contact/impact, near misses, unsafe trajectories), perception loss/recovery, intervention/abort rate, and compute/energy. Publish failures and confidence intervals, and measure ranking stability across conditions. The opportunity weakens if existing shared protocols already capture comparable vectors and methods' rankings remain stable when harm and task outcomes are jointly reported.
limitations: Only four of twelve records in this sample cell were audited here; six remain unread and two were covered earlier. This is a candidate measurement gap, not a systematic review of robotics safety protocols or a pooled estimate. Trial counts in some hardware studies are too small to estimate rare damage rates.

topic: robotics; inverse reinforcement learning; reward hacking; human feedback
status: bounded candidate evaluation opportunity; support exists in two research lineages but a matched replicated physical exploit test remains unverified
claim: A sampled 2026 IRL paper uses progress labels to shape rewards and demonstrates improved responses in two selected simulated reward-hacking scenarios. Its cited antecedent supports progress as a human signal for task completion/backtracking (116 participants; 40 non-expert demonstrations). An independent 2025 method, ReWiND, evaluates reward ordering on failure/near-success/success rollouts and reports real-robot task gains. Thus reward robustness and physical outcomes are already studied; the narrower question is whether these reward models resist held-out adversarial exploits reproducibly on hardware while preserving task success and safety. PHIRL reports one training run per condition, and ReWiND relies on supervised resets/success detection and reports a failure case under bimanual occlusion.
positive_evidence: PHIRL reports two Robosuite reward-hacking scenarios: repeated lift-drop under AIRL and poke-without-place under environmental reward; progress shaping penalizes the drop loop and gives near-zero negative reward to poking.
The PHIRL paper reports 100 simulation evaluation rollouts, but explicitly reports one training run per condition; this leaves training variability unmeasured.

The 2025 progress-feedback study includes 76 online participants and 40 non-expert demonstrators; 34/40 public-space demonstrations ultimately succeed despite varied policies, and progress annotations track task completion/backtracking in the studied tasks.

Independent ReWiND work scores failure, near-success, and success rollouts across 17 unseen simulation tasks; on five real-robot tasks, mean success rises from 12% for the pretrained policy to 68% after an hour of online reward-guided learning.
counterevidence: The 2025 human-progress study tests task completion, harmless/fixable errors, unproductive behavior, and backtracking; ReWiND evaluates failed rollouts and real-robot task outcomes. Therefore it would be false to say reward robustness or physical outcomes are generally unstudied.

ReWiND's rollout robustness evidence ranks selected failure/near-success/success clips rather than using a held-out adversarial exploit suite with safety endpoints; online learning assumes human resets and success detection.
ReWiND reports a bimanual dish-scrubbing reward-alignment failure associated with missing bimanual training data and camera occlusion; PHIRL's two hacks remain qualitative selected simulation cases.

§§IV–V online/public-space studies; §VI discussion of reward hacking
§§4.1–4.2 reward alignment and policy learning; §5 limitations; appendices C/D real-robot protocol and failure analysis

falsifiable_test: Pre-register a matched comparison of progress/rubric shaping, ReWiND-style video reward learning, preference-based reward learning, and plain reward baselines. Hold out attack templates (cyclic reward loops, harmless-but-nonprogress actions, and visually occluded or semantically shifted tasks), run at least five independent training seeds, and test in simulation and on hardware. Report task success, exploit frequency/severity, contact or near-miss outcomes, intervention/reset dependence, and human annotation cost separately. The opportunity weakens if independent prior work already reports stable, replicated physical robustness against held-out exploit patterns.
limitations: This is a focused citation trace of three papers across two lineages, not a systematic review. The human-progress study validates a feedback signal; ReWiND shows categorized rollout and physical-task evidence but not the exact held-out exploit/safety protocol; PHIRL uses selected qualitative hacks and one training run per condition. No field-wide absence claim is justified.
